title: PowerPoint's Built-in Video Export vs a Dedicated Converter (blog explainer)

brief.story: A clear explainer of the post.

slides.title: Built-in Export vs a Dedicated Converter
slides.notes: Want to save PowerPoint as video? You have two sensible options, and they suit different jobs. Here's how to pick the right one for your deck.

slides.title: Built-in export keeps your own voice
bullets: Recorded timings or fixed seconds per slide
slides.notes: PowerPoint's own export plays your animations exactly as designed, with your real voice. The catch? Stumble on slide 12, and you re-record slide 12.

slides.title: A converter treats video as its own thing
bullets: Edit the notes and export again
slides.notes: A dedicated converter reads your speaker notes aloud, adds captions and times everything to the speech. The trade-off is a synthetic voice instead of your own.

slides.title: The same slide, two ways
bullets: "New starters get their laptop on day one"
Built-in: record it, re-record when it changes
Converter: type it into the notes, edit and export again
slides.notes: Take one headline about new starters' laptops. Record it yourself, and every change means a new take. Type it into the notes, and a change is one quick edit.

slides.title: Quick checklist for choosing
bullets: Captions without extra work? Dedicated converter
slides.notes: Many people use both. A leader's quarterly message suits their own voice, while an onboarding module that changes every few months suits a converter.
